video_title: Why Money Launderers Love $100 Bills | Odd Lots
gist: Journalist Oliver Bullough argues the $200bn/year global anti-money-laundering compliance apparatus has failed — laundering has held steady at 2-5% of global GDP since the late 1990s — because the real flows happen outside regulated banks, in cash smuggling, trade-based value transfer and stablecoins. He ties this to the 'paradox of banknotes': cash use in transactions has collapsed to roughly 9-13% while US currency in circulation approaches $2.5 trillion, 85% of it $100 bills, because seigniorage makes central banks structurally uninterested in killing high-denomination notes.

insights.claim: The standard estimate that 2-5% of global GDP is laundered annually — roughly $2-5 trillion against a ~$100 trillion world economy — traces back to a late-1990s guesstimate by IMF head Michel Camdessus and has never been revised.
insights.speaker: Oliver Bullough
insights.so_what: The headline number underpinning the entire AML compliance industry is a 30-year-old approximation, so any thesis or regulation built on it rests on far weaker foundations than its ubiquity implies.
insights.quote: the most widely used estimate is that we're talking about between 2 and 5% of global GDP

insights.claim: The fact that the laundered share of global GDP is unchanged since the 1990s implies decades of AML effort achieved nothing beyond preventing the criminal economy from growing as a share — criminals have matched regulators step for step.
insights.speaker: Oliver Bullough
insights.so_what: Frames AML spending as a cost center with no measurable output — a policy area ripe for either abandonment or radical redesign, and a headwind for vendors selling more of the same.
insights.quote: criminals have been able to outmaneuver regulators and law enforcement agencies and governments attempts to limit them

insights.claim: Global AML compliance costs roughly $200 billion a year according to LexisNexis, an amount that would cover solving world hunger plus clean water and sanitation for everyone on Earth with about $50 billion left over.
insights.speaker: Oliver Bullough
insights.so_what: Sizes the compliance-tech and staffing market while arguing its ROI is near zero — relevant both to regtech valuations and to the political durability of the spend.
insights.quote: the estimates from LexisNexis is that global compliance with AML legislation, it costs something like $200 billion a year

insights.claim: Laundering through regulated banks is a small slice of the total: Danske Bank was accused of moving about $130 billion over several years for suspicious Russian clients, while global cash smuggling alone runs into the hundreds of billions annually and trade-based laundering is estimated at roughly $1 trillion a year.
insights.speaker: Oliver Bullough
insights.so_what: Bank-focused enforcement is watching the smallest channel; the real exposure sits in customs, trade finance and physical cash logistics — a mis-set regulatory perimeter.
insights.quote: global cash smuggling is certainly in the hundreds of billions annually

insights.claim: Criminal networks move value rather than money — mis-invoiced manufactured goods, tractors, luxury handbags or drugs — because cross-border checks apply to money transfers, not to shipments of stuff.
insights.speaker: Oliver Bullough
insights.so_what: Explains why enforcement aimed at payment rails is structurally blind, and why trade-finance and customs data are the underexploited surveillance frontier.
insights.quote: You don't need to move money internationally because that's where the checks are on transactions. You just move value internationally in the form of luxury goods, cocaine or, or, you know, illicit goods of whatever kind.

insights.claim: Cartel books must balance, so drug inflows into the US are offset by outbound flows of American-made capital goods such as Caterpillar and John Deere equipment, alongside roughly $25 billion of physical cash smuggled into Mexico each year.
insights.speaker: Oliver Bullough
insights.so_what: A slice of US heavy-equipment and luxury export demand is illicit-flow-driven, meaning aggressive enforcement or de-dollarization of cartel finance is a latent demand risk for those exporters.
insights.quote: $25 billion worth of cash is smuggled into Mexico every year

insights.claim: China's $50,000 per person per year capital-export limit creates persistent offshore demand for cash among wealthy Chinese, which brokers match against the cash surplus generated by Western drug prohibition — the 'Vancouver model.'
insights.speaker: Oliver Bullough
insights.so_what: Chinese capital controls are effectively subsidizing global cartel finance; any loosening or tightening of the $50k limit changes the economics of drug-money laundering worldwide.
insights.quote: the basis of the trade is that there is a restriction on moving money out of China, or $50,000 per person per year

insights.claim: The Vancouver model has scaled from a bilateral Canada-China arrangement into a global triangular trade — luxury goods from Europe to China, goods from China to South America, cocaine from South America to Europe — with no international money movement required.
insights.speaker: Oliver Bullough
insights.so_what: Describes a parallel settlement system immune to SWIFT-level sanctions, which limits the reach of financial sanctions as a policy tool.
insights.quote: this happens globally on a truly colossal scale

insights.claim: Modern laundering replicates Medici banking, which settled cross-Alpine obligations by moving silk, spices and wool and hiding cash movements inside trade paperwork rather than shipping bullion.
insights.speaker: Oliver Bullough
insights.so_what: A reminder that netting-plus-goods settlement is the historical default, not an aberration — useful when assessing which 'novel' fintech settlement designs are actually old and durable.
insights.quote: they were just hiding the movement of cash in the paperwork

insights.claim: The binding constraint criminals optimize for is value density — dollar value per unit of spatial volume — which is why $100 bills, Rolexes and jewels recur while bulky goods do not.
insights.speaker: Joe Weisenthal
insights.so_what: A screening lens for which asset classes attract illicit demand — and thus which face future regulatory attention: watches, gems, art, high-denomination notes.
insights.quote: you use a metric that is very rarely ever discussed in economics, which is dollar value per unit of spatial volume

insights.claim: A $1 million watch can be worn across a border and sold at the other end with no declaration, while $10,000 in cash must be declared — an enforcement asymmetry that persists unaddressed.
insights.speaker: Tracy Alloway
insights.so_what: Points to luxury hard assets as the likeliest next target of AML rulemaking, a regulatory risk for high-end watch and jewelry retail.
insights.quote: It is kind of crazy that you have to declare, like, more than $10,000 in cash at the airport, but you could easily have a $1 million watch on your wrist.

insights.claim: Cash is used in only about 9% of UK transactions and roughly 13% in the US, yet currency in circulation keeps hitting records — nearly $2.5 trillion in the US, about €1.6 trillion in the eurozone and roughly £100 billion in the UK.
insights.speaker: Oliver Bullough
insights.so_what: Currency in circulation is not a proxy for consumer cash demand; models that treat rising CIC as a payments or trust signal are mis-specified.
insights.quote: I think it's like something like 9% now in the UK, maybe 13% in the US

insights.claim: The store-of-value explanation central banks give for rising cash fails their own survey data: the average American adult holds about $430 on hand, while more than $7,000 per capita is outstanding — an order-of-magnitude gap left unexplained.
insights.speaker: Oliver Bullough
insights.so_what: The unexplained ~95% of circulating currency is the single largest unmeasured monetary aggregate; whoever explains it reprices the seigniorage and illicit-finance debate.
insights.quote: the average American adult has, I think something like 430 odd dollars, either on that person or at home at any one time. And yet there's more than $7,000 out there for every man, woman and child in the United States.

insights.claim: The three explanations Andrew Bailey offered in 2009 for the banknote paradox — low interest rates removing opportunity cost, ATM stockpiling, and post-crisis distrust of banks — have all reversed while the phenomenon accelerated; pounds in circulation have doubled since that speech.
insights.speaker: Oliver Bullough
insights.so_what: Falsifies the benign macro explanations for cash growth and strengthens the illicit-demand hypothesis, which has different policy tail risks.
insights.quote: the value of pounds in circulation, for example, has doubled since he made that speech

insights.claim: Roughly half of euro banknotes sit outside the eurozone and the Fed estimates about 65% of dollar banknotes are outside the United States, which relocates the puzzle geographically rather than answering it.
insights.speaker: Oliver Bullough
insights.so_what: Offshore dollar cash demand is a real, large and poorly understood component of dollar dominance — relevant to any de-dollarization thesis.
insights.quote: The fed reckons sort of something like 65%, maybe, dollar banknotes are outside the United States

insights.claim: The correct way to understand seigniorage is not the ~$99.91 margin on printing a $100 bill but that $2.5 trillion of outstanding currency is an interest-free loan to the US government — roughly 6% of a nearly $40 trillion debt stack, saving perhaps a percentage point on a debt-service bill already near 19% of the federal budget.
insights.speaker: Oliver Bullough
insights.so_what: Quantifies why Washington has a fiscal incentive to keep high-denomination cash alive — a structural obstacle to any $100-bill withdrawal, and a hidden support for debt sustainability math.
insights.quote: it's an interest free loan to the government is what it really is

insights.claim: Because 85% of the roughly $2.4 trillion of US currency in circulation is in $100 bills, the currency stock is dominated by a denomination almost no one uses in daily life.
insights.speaker: Tracy Alloway
insights.so_what: The composition, not just the level, of currency growth is the tell — track $100-bill share as the cleanest public proxy for illicit cash demand.
insights.quote: 85% of the $2.4 trillion in circulation happens to be $100 bills

insights.claim: Carousel or missing-trader intra-community fraud exploits the EU rule that cross-border goods trade is zero-rated for VAT: goods are imported VAT-free, sold through a domestic shell that vanishes without remitting the ~20% VAT, then re-exported by a second shell that reclaims that never-paid VAT from the treasury.
insights.speaker: Oliver Bullough
insights.so_what: A design flaw that manufactures 20% of shipment value from nothing and is structurally unfixable without cross-border tax-authority trust — a permanent fiscal leak in EU budgets.
insights.quote: you've essentially conjured up 20% of the value of a shipment from thin air

insights.claim: Unlike most acquisitive crime, carousel fraud has no natural ceiling and no reason for gangs to compete, so participants collaborate to build ever more elaborate multi-thousand-shell-company chains.
insights.speaker: Oliver Bullough
insights.so_what: Uncapped, non-rivalrous fraud economics predict explosive growth wherever the loophole exists — a template for spotting similar unbounded subsidy or credit-refund exploits.
insights.quote: essentially there is no limit to the amount of money that that a criminal gang can make out of this

insights.claim: The UK largely defeated carousel fraud using a full multi-agency state effort rather than outsourcing detection to banks, but the fraud simply migrated to the rest of Europe where it is now roughly a €50 billion a year problem stretching from Lithuania to Portugal.
insights.speaker: Oliver Bullough
insights.so_what: Demonstrates both that state-led enforcement works and that unilateral success only relocates the crime — the core jurisdictional-arbitrage problem in all financial-crime policy.
insights.quote: it just crossed into the rest of Europe, where now it's a, you know, a €50 billion a year problem, carousel fraud

insights.claim: Crypto's role in money laundering is specifically a stablecoin story, not a general crypto story, with stablecoins serving as the instantaneous digital equivalent of moving value as goods.
insights.speaker: Oliver Bullough
insights.so_what: Concentrates regulatory tail risk on stablecoin issuers rather than crypto broadly — the key exposure to watch in any stablecoin-linked investment.
insights.quote: specifically, we're really talking about stablecoins when we talk about crypto being big in in money laundering

insights.claim: Cash and crypto are complements rather than substitutes for sophisticated Russian, Chinese and Iranian networks: cash is collected at street level then converted to crypto for cross-border movement, because cash is bulky, insecure and hard to count.
insights.speaker: Oliver Bullough
insights.so_what: Undercuts the argument that crypto adoption reduces cash-based crime — it raises the throughput of both, so cash and crypto enforcement must be sequenced together.
insights.quote: the two are not, exclusive. In fact, they supercharge each other

insights.claim: Russia has created its own cryptocurrency, described as A75 and currently in some trouble, specifically to operate outside Western-controlled stablecoins.
insights.speaker: Oliver Bullough
insights.so_what: Sanctioned states are building parallel stablecoin rails, a live test of whether dollar-stablecoin dominance extends to adversary jurisdictions.
insights.quote: the Russians have been, you know, created their own cryptocurrency, A75, although it's it's in a little bit of trouble at the moment

insights.claim: Because stablecoin reserves are largely invested in US Treasuries, laundering that runs through stablecoins recreates the seigniorage dynamic — the US collects a cheap funding benefit and therefore has weak incentive to crack down.
insights.speaker: Tracy Alloway
insights.so_what: Predicts persistent US regulatory forbearance toward stablecoins on fiscal-funding grounds — bullish for issuer durability, bearish for expecting hard enforcement.

insights.claim: Apparently bilateral transactions are usually multi-leg chains that can be decomposed and rearranged like Lego blocks, and every additional leg is a distinct exploitable vulnerability.
insights.speaker: Joe Weisenthal
insights.so_what: A general lens for finding where value leaks in any payment or settlement architecture — count the legs, then find which one lacks a check.
insights.quote: a lot of times what looks like a transaction is really like this big multi leg transaction that could sort of be decomposed and rearranged like Lego blocks

insights.claim: Despite the euro offering twice the value density via its €200 note, the $100 bill remains the lingua franca of global criminality because dollar cash is a deeper, more liquid, more universally accepted market — a first-mover advantage mirroring the dollar's licit reserve role.
insights.speaker: Oliver Bullough
insights.so_what: Network effects entrench the dollar in the illicit economy as firmly as in the licit one, adding an overlooked structural floor under offshore dollar demand.
insights.quote: the dollar remains, you know, the, the lingua franca of of global criminality, the hundred dollar bill, just because it is a much deeper, more liquid market

insights.claim: In 1990s Russia, $100 bills fetched a better ruble exchange rate than $20 bills, showing a real price premium on denomination driven purely by demand for high-value notes.
insights.speaker: Oliver Bullough
insights.so_what: Denomination premia are an observable, tradeable market signal of illicit or capital-flight cash demand in a given jurisdiction.
insights.quote: I knew I could get more rubles in front of dollar bill than I could for a 20

insights.claim: China's highest-denomination note is 100 RMB, worth only about $15, in sharp contrast to the $100 bill and €500 note — a deliberate design contrast in a currency that also keeps a single uniform Mao design across denominations.
insights.speaker: Joe Weisenthal
insights.so_what: China exports capital-flight demand rather than high-value banknotes, which is precisely why Chinese laundering networks intermediate other currencies' cash.

insights.claim: Eliminating high-denomination notes is a collective action problem: a unilateral US withdrawal of the $100 bill would simply push criminals to €100 and €200 notes, transferring seigniorage to Europe with no reduction in crime, so only an international agreement — which has so far eluded everyone — would work.
insights.speaker: Oliver Bullough
insights.so_what: Explains why Rogoff-style proposals to kill big bills have gone nowhere and why they should be treated as a very low-probability policy risk to cash-dependent businesses.
insights.quote: if one of them went out the game, it essentially wouldn't make that much difference to the criminals, but would make a substantial difference to their own income

insights.claim: The profits of enabling financial crime accrue locally while the harms are exported, so the City of London has profited for decades and the US profits from $100-bill demand while Colombia and Mexico bear the damage.
insights.speaker: Oliver Bullough
insights.so_what: A durable externality structure that predicts continued non-cooperation — jurisdictions with the largest enabling profits will keep defecting from reform.
insights.quote: So you get the profit and other people get the harm.

insights.claim: Withdrawal of high-denomination notes has precedent — Europe stopped producing the €500 note, nicknamed the bin Laden because everyone had heard of it but no one had seen it, after the Paris attacks — showing the policy is feasible when political will exists.
insights.speaker: Oliver Bullough
insights.so_what: Establishes a terrorism-shock trigger as the realistic catalyst for high-denomination withdrawal, rather than steady-state AML policy.
insights.quote: which was referred to colloquially as the bin laden because everyone had heard of it, but no one had seen it

insights.claim: Suspicious activity reports were designed in 1989 as real-time law-enforcement intelligence but most countries never resourced agencies to read them, so reports flow into a black hole while banks face billion-dollar-plus fines for misses and no upside for hits.
insights.speaker: Oliver Bullough
insights.so_what: A pure-downside incentive structure guarantees defensive over-reporting; the fix — fewer reports actually read — would shrink compliance headcount and regtech volume.
insights.quote: it would be far better to have fewer suspicious activity reports that were actually being read

insights.claim: Debanking is a serious and under-discussed side effect of AML and counter-terrorist-financing rules, affecting hundreds of thousands of people globally, mostly Muslims.
insights.speaker: Oliver Bullough
insights.so_what: A growing political and litigation risk for banks that use blunt de-risking as the cheapest compliance response.

insights.claim: The Bank Secrecy Act of 1970 arose from one congressman's personal obsession — Texas Democrat Patman, chair of the House Banking Committee, whose distrust of monopoly and financial institutions gave him the hierarchical power to push it through — and no comparable political entrepreneur exists today.
insights.speaker: Oliver Bullough
insights.so_what: Major AML reform is champion-dependent, not consensus-driven, so absent an individual sponsor the status quo persists — low probability of regime change in the near term.

insights.claim: Governments run contradictory policies: they impose expensive AML regulation on financial institutions while simultaneously printing effectively limitless banknotes that let criminals bypass those same restrictions.
insights.speaker: Oliver Bullough
insights.so_what: The single sharpest framing of policy incoherence in financial crime — useful for anticipating that AML costs will keep rising without effectiveness gains.
insights.quote: they are simultaneously printing essentially limitless quantities of banknotes that are allowing criminals to evade those same restrictions by just using cash
